name: Triton Inference Server
notable_features: The general-purpose inference server, from before the LLM serving era, and still the default answer for 'I have many different models on many different frameworks'. vLLM and friends are LLM engines; Triton is the substrate they could sit on
Dynamic batching AND sequence batching with implicit state management for stateful models - the sequence batcher is the thing that made Triton relevant to LLM serving before paged attention existed
Concurrent model execution: many models on one GPU with automatic concurrency
Backend API for custom backends, plus Python-based backends as the in-process extension point. This is how you get a new framework onto Triton without C++
Model ensembles and Business Logic Scripting for multi-stage pipelines (preprocess, ensemble, postprocess) declared in the model repository rather than coded
Multi-framework: PyTorch, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python, RAPIDS FIL and more per the README
Runs on NVIDIA GPUs, x86 and ARM CPU, or AWS Inferentia, across cloud, data center, edge and embedded
HTTP/REST and gRPC protocols; filesystem model repository with explicit model-control mode
Part of NVIDIA AI Enterprise, which is the commercial context for support
BSD-3-Clause, which is a genuine contrast with the AGPL/NOASSERTION licences elsewhere in this slice
11042 stars, v2.73.0 released 2026-09-30 (the 26.09 container on NGC), last push 2026-10-03, 4163 open issues
hardware_caveats: NOT AN LLM ENGINE. Triton has no paged KV, no prefix caching, no speculative decoding and no token-level scheduling. If you are serving LLMs at scale you want vLLM or SGLang; Triton is what you deploy when the answer is 'a directory of heterogeneous models'

Vendor lock-in is the central design fact: the model repository format, the backends, the container releases and the support path are all NVIDIA's, and the README explicitly places Triton inside NVIDIA AI Enterprise

The 26.09 container release and the r26.09 git branch are the versioning coupling to watch - README instructions clone branch r26.09, so Triton version lines track NVIDIA's calendar not semver cadence

Python backends run in-process and are the pragmatic way to add a framework, but they are also the fastest way to hit GIL-bound throughput on a token loop. Fine for ensembles, bad for hot per-token paths

Backend maturity is uneven and version-specific. TensorRT plan files are locked to a specific TensorRT version; ONNX Runtime and OpenVINO backends track their own upstream. The 'supports many frameworks' claim is a list of independently-versioned dependencies
Inferentia support is AWS-specific and inherently narrow
4163 open issues; as a 2018-vintage project the accumulated surface is large
README feature claims are NVIDIA's own - the 'optimized performance' framing is vendor language and no per-model numbers are given
best_for: Serving a portfolio of many different models from many different frameworks behind one HTTP/gRPC contract - Triton's actual design target
Non-LLM workloads at scale: vision, speech, recommendation, classical ML alongside a couple of LLMs
Multi-stage inference pipelines where preprocessing, the model and postprocessing belong in one declared ensemble
Deploying to AWS Inferentia, or to edge/embedded NVIDIA hardware
Teams already licensed to NVIDIA AI Enterprise who want a supported substrate under their generative workloads
avoid_for: LLM serving at scale - no paged KV, no prefix caching, no speculative decoding. Use vLLM or SGLang
Token-level throughput work where a Python backend's GIL is the bottleneck
Portability beyond NVIDIA's ecosystem, unless you value the framework breadth enough to accept the model-repository format
TensorRT plan-file portability - plans are version-locked
notes: Included as the pre-LLM general-purpose server that the whole serving ecosystem grew around, and as the honest answer to 'why not just use Triton'. Its sequence batcher and implicit state management predate paged attention and are the historically interesting part. BSD-3-Clause, 2018 vintage, r26.09 branch/container coupling, and the AI Enterprise context are all recorded because they bear on adoption. See [[ev-maintenance-status-is-four-dated-facts]] for how to read this fact set. tracing_support set to per-request on 2026-10-04: Triton exposes OpenTelemetry as an alternative trace backend (--trace-config mode=opentelemetry --trace-config opentelemetry,url=<endpoint>) with context propagation supported, and its documented minimal trace is 3 spans - top level, model and compute - carrying model_name, model_version, request_id and parent_id (obs-triton-trace-doc). Not per-phase: the three spans are nesting levels of one request, not prefill and decode, and Triton core has no phase-level tracing concept. Note the clock caveat carried from the same doc: OTel timestamps use the system clock while Triton's own trace API uses a steady clock, so the two modes are not numerically comparable.
